How to Play Sushi Go! (Rules and Scoring)

2026-11-12

How to play Sushi Go!: everyone picks one card, everyone passes the rest, and you score whatever you keep. Highest total after three rounds wins. It plays 2 to 5 people in about 15 minutes, works for ages 8 and up, and costs $11.99.

If you only remember one thing from this page, remember this. Sushi Go! is not a game about the card you take. It is a game about the card you leave, because every pick hands the next player a smaller and worse hand. The last two cards of a round are usually worth nothing, and whoever planned for that wins.

I have taught this to maybe 40 people, most of them at parties where nobody wanted to read rules. It takes one round for the whole table to get it. I still lose about a third of my games to my girlfriend, who has never once counted a maki roll out loud.

The Goal, in One Line

Score more points than everyone else after three rounds. That is the whole objective. There is no board, no map, and no player pieces. The 108 cards are the game.

There is one tiebreak. If two players finish level, the one with more pudding cards wins. Which tells you something about how much this game cares about dessert.

What Is in the Box

108 cards and 12 different types. The exact count matters, because the numbers explain the strategy better than any guide.

14 tempura. 14 sashimi. 14 dumpling. 12 two-maki rolls. 8 three-maki rolls. 6 one-maki rolls. 10 salmon nigiri. 5 squid nigiri. 5 egg nigiri. 10 pudding. 6 wasabi. 4 chopsticks.

Pay attention to this number: 4. There are only four chopsticks cards in the entire box, and I will come back to why that matters.

Setup in 60 Seconds

Shuffle all 108 cards. Deal a starting hand based on player count. Two players get 10 cards each, three players get 9, four players get 8, and five players get 7. Everything left over goes face down as the draw pile.

Then grab paper and a pencil and pick a scorekeeper. That is the entire setup. There is no board to lay out and nothing to punch out of cardboard.

The dealing step is doing more work than it looks. A smaller hand at a bigger table means fewer choices per player, so the five-player game is a different game from the three-player one, not just a longer one.

Your Turn: Pick One, Pass the Rest

Every turn works the same way. Look at your hand, choose one card, and place it face down in front of you. When everyone has picked, everyone flips at the same time. Then you pass the cards you did not choose to the player on your left.

Pick up your new hand, choose another card, reveal, pass again. Keep going until the hands run out. Then score everything sitting face up in front of you. That is one round. Deal a fresh hand and do it twice more.

Yes, it really is that light. The whole turn is two decisions: keep this, pass that.

What Every Card Scores

Here is the full scoring list, sorted the way you will actually use it.

CardScores
Maki rolls (1, 2 or 3 icons)Most icons: 6. Second most: 3
TempuraSet of 2: 5
SashimiSet of 3: 10
Dumplings1: 1. 2: 3. 3: 6. 4: 10. 5 or more: 15
Egg nigiri1
Salmon nigiri2
Squid nigiri3
WasabiScores nothing. Triples the next nigiri placed on it
Chopsticks0
PuddingScored at the end. Most: plus 6. Fewest: minus 6

Maki is the only card in the game that pays based on what everyone else has. Everything else pays for what you collect. That single difference is where most beginner mistakes live.

The Math Nobody Runs: Points per Card

Here is the key insight. Rank every play by points per card instead of total points, and the game changes shape.

PlayCards usedPoints per card
Squid nigiri on wasabi24.5
Full sashimi set33.33
Salmon nigiri on wasabi23.0
Plain squid nigiri13.0
Tempura pair22.5
Four dumplings42.5
Plain salmon nigiri12.0
Maki, if you win the race32.0

Most beginners chase maki because the trophy is printed on the card. Look at that last row. Maki pays about 2 points per card if you win, and it is the most contested thing in the box. Three players spend three cards each, one player scores 6, one scores 3, and one scores nothing for the same effort. A single plain squid nigiri, taken quietly while everyone fights over maki, is worth more per card than winning the whole maki race.

However, the math has one trap. Full sashimi is the second-best rate in the game at 3.33 points per card, but only if you land all three. Two sashimi score zero. I have watched people spend a whole round chasing the third one and finish with nothing but two useless cards.

Wasabi: The Rule Beginners Get Wrong

Here is the honest part about wasabi, and it is the rule I see broken most at new tables. Wasabi scores nothing on its own. Place it in front of you, and the next nigiri you take has to sit on top of it. That nigiri is then worth triple.

Squid goes from 3 to 9. Salmon goes from 2 to 6. Egg goes from 1 to 3. A wasabi with no nigiri on it at the end of the round scores nothing at all.

Two small rules matter here. You may hold several wasabi cards at once, but only one nigiri can land on each one. And the best pairing in the game is the expensive one: squid on wasabi is 9 points for two cards, which beats every other play on the board.

Then Comes the Card That Scores Zero

I thought I had this game figured out after my tenth play. Then I stopped counting points and started counting turns.

Here is the contradiction. The single biggest payout in the game is 15 points from five dumplings. The card that decides the most games in my notebook is worth a hard zero. It is chopsticks.

Chopsticks does nothing on its own. It sits in front of you and scores nothing. But on a later turn you can call out "Sushi Go!" before anyone else reveals, take a second card from your hand, and place both face down. Then the chopsticks goes back into your hand, which means it gets passed on, and everyone else can take it and use it too.

Why it wins games: it is the only card in the box that lets you finish an all-or-nothing set in a single turn. Two sashimi in one hand is the dream every Sushi Go! player is chasing, and chopsticks is the only way to take both. It also breaks the tempo, because you take two cards while everyone else takes one, so the hand you pass on is smaller than anyone expected. Remember the four-card count from the top of this page. There are four of these in the box and most tables treat them as junk.

However, chopsticks has a real cost. You can only use one per turn even if you are holding three, and every turn you hold it you are playing with one fewer scoring card in front of you. Take it in round three and you will probably never cash it in.

The Variant Most Tables Never Use

The rules include an optional rule that changes the game more than any expansion. Pass both ways. In rounds one and three, pass left. In round two, pass right.

Most groups pass left all three rounds and never notice the option. Alternating direction flips the player on your right into someone you have to read.

Here is why that matters. In a left-passing game you only ever see the hands of the person sitting to your right, and you learn their habits. Turn round two around and a whole second neighbor enters the picture, so the cards you can safely leave behind change. My group switched two months ago, and the second round is now the one people argue about.

The 2-Player Variant, and the Pudding Rule Nobody Knows

The box handles two players with a dummy hand. Deal three hands of nine cards. One hand sits face down between you as a dummy pile.

The player who controls the dummy draws the top card of the pile into their own hand, then picks one card for themselves and one for the dummy. Your opponent plays one card as normal. Reveal, switch hands, and the dummy pile stays in place. Control passes back and forth every turn.

Then the rule that surprises everyone. In a two-player game, nobody loses points for pudding. Only the player with the most pudding scores the 6.

At three players and up, pudding cuts both ways. Most pudding is plus 6, and fewest pudding is minus 6, including players who took none at all. That one card turns a friendly round into a real decision: take a pudding you do not want, or risk losing 6 points at the end. I have watched a player lose a game by exactly the 6 points they never took.

What to Buy, and What to Skip

So now you know how to play. The next question is which box to put on the table.

The original Sushi Go! is $11.99. That is the whole game: 2 to 5 players, a tin box, 15 minutes, and no expansions required. The full specs and current price live on my Sushi Go! page.

If your game night runs bigger, look at Sushi Go Party!. It plays 2 to 8 people, runs about 20 minutes, and it runs $21.99. It is a standalone game, not an expansion. Same designer, Phil Walker-Harding, but instead of one fixed deck it hands you a menu you build before each game, so you choose which card types are in play. The Sushi Go Party! page has the full breakdown.

For a drafting game with more weight behind it, 7 Wonders takes the same pick-and-pass idea and builds a whole civilization around it. It is the natural next step once Sushi Go starts feeling solved, and my how to play 7 Wonders guide walks through it.

The Honest Truth About Sushi Go!

Here is the honest truth. Sushi Go! is a solitaire game with witnesses. You cannot attack anyone, you cannot block a set someone else is building, and you cannot take a card off another player's pile. Everyone builds their own meal, and the only interaction is deciding what to leave behind.

That is a genuine weakness. If your group likes take-that games and table talk, this will feel quiet. There is no villain and no drama.

Two more things worth naming. A five-player game deals only 7 cards each, so long plans get cut short, and that is the weakest player count in the box. And the game has a ceiling. Once everyone at the table can run the points-per-card math, the maki race becomes obvious and rounds get tighter. I would not plan a whole evening around it.

For a 15-minute closer, though, quiet is the point. It is the game you pull out when energy is dipping and nobody wants to learn anything heavy.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this game survive ten plays on a shelf that already holds 40 boxes?

Sushi Go! passes on speed. Fifteen minutes, a tin box that fits in a backpack, and a teach that takes one round. It is the game I hand to a group that has never played anything modern, and it has never failed to land. I have played it more than 60 times and I still set it up without thinking.

Sushi Go Party! passes for a different reason. The menu means the deck changes between game nights, so ten plays of Party is ten slightly different games. That is the box I would buy if my group is usually six or more.

The honest bar: if you cannot picture playing it twice in one night, it does not earn the shelf space. Sushi Go! earns it. Fifteen minutes is short enough that you will.

Here is the part that matters. Grab Sushi Go! at about $11.99 for a small table, or Sushi Go Party! at $21.99 if your game night runs six or more. Prices bounce, so catch the original under $13 and Party under $23 and you have done well. New to the hobby?
